name: Afrikaans
family: Indo-European, Germanic, West Germanic, Low Franconian (daughter of 17th-century Dutch)
variety: Standard Afrikaans of South Africa, in the form described by Wissing (2020) and Donaldson (1993); regional and ethnolectal differences are noted
sources: Wissing, Daan (2020). Afrikaans. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 50(1), 127-140.
Donaldson, Bruce C. (1993). A Grammar of Afrikaans. Berlin: Mouton de Gruyter.
Donaldson, Bruce (1994). Afrikaans. In König and van der Auwera (eds.), The Germanic Languages. London: Routledge.
Le Roux, T. H. and Pienaar, P. de Villiers (1927). Afrikaanse fonetiek. Cape Town: Juta.
Combrink, J. G. H. and de Stadler, L. G. (1987). Afrikaanse fonologie. Johannesburg: Macmillan.
Lass, Roger (1987). Intradiphthongal dependencies. In Anderson and Durand (eds.), Explorations in Dependency Phonology. Dordrecht: Foris.

Coetzee, Andries W.; Beddor, Patrice Speeter; Shedden, Kerby; Styler, Will; Wissing, Daan (2018). Plosive voicing in Afrikaans: differential cue weighting and tonogenesis. Journal of Phonetics 66, 185-216.
contrasts: short /a/ versus long /ɑː/ (man versus maan), which also differ in quality
short mid vowels versus the long mid vowels, which are centring diphthongs: /ɛ/ versus /ɪə/ (bed, beet), /ɔ/ versus /ʊə/ (bom, boom), /œ/ versus /øə/ (put, neus)
a stressable schwa /ə/ (written i: sit, kind) versus /i/ (written ie: siek) and /ɛ/
front rounded /y øə œ œi/ versus unrounded /i ɪə ə əi/, a contrast that many speakers weaken or give up
three closing diphthongs /əi œi œu/ (ys, huis, koud)
voiced versus voiceless plosives /b d/ versus /p t/ in onsets, neutralised at the end of a word; the contrast is cued more and more by pitch on the following vowel
/f/ versus /v/ (vier versus wier); native words have no /z/
allophony: the long mid vowels are centring diphthongs [ɪə øə ʊə] (weet, seun, boom)
/ɛ/ is lowered to [æ] before /k χ l r/ (ek [æk], weg [væχ], vel [fæl], werk [værk]), and /ɛː/ to [æː] before /r/ (perd [pæːrt], wêreld); the lowering is most regular in the north of the country
a vowel before /n/ plus a fricative, above all /s/, is nasalised and lengthened and the /n/ is lost: ons [ɔ̃ːs], mens [mɛ̃ːs], kans [kɑ̃ːs], Afrikaans [afriˈkɑ̃ːs]
front rounded vowels are unrounded by many speakers: /y/ to [i], /øə/ to [eə] or [ɪə], /œ/ to [ə], /œi/ to [əi]
/i y u/ are short, but long before /r/ (vier [fiːr], muur [myːr], boer [buːr])
/b d/ are often produced without prevoicing, mostly by younger speakers; the following vowel then starts on a lower pitch than after /p t/
final devoicing: obstruents are voiceless at the end of a word (hond [ɦɔnt] beside honde [ˈɦɔndə], rib [rəp])
/χ/ is usually uvular, a fricative or a voiceless trill; velar [x] is also heard, mainly next to front vowels
/r/ is an alveolar trill or tap; a uvular r ('bry') is regional, in the Swartland and neighbouring parts of the Western Cape
/v/ (written w) is [v], but [w] after an obstruent in the same syllable (twee [twɪə], kwaad [kwɑːt], swart)
/k/ is palatal [c] in the diminutive ending -tjie, -djie [ci], and the vowel before it gains a palatal offglide or is raised: katjie [ˈkaici], hondjie [ˈɦɔiɲci], voetjie [ˈfuici]
/n/ assimilates in place to a following consonant
schwa [ə] is the vowel of most unstressed syllables
phonotactics: final clusters are simpler than in Dutch, because /t/ was lost after obstruents (nag, lug, kos against Dutch nacht, lucht, kost); it returns before a vowel-initial suffix in some words (nagte)
onset clusters of up to three consonants, the first being /s/ (spr, str, skr)
/ɦ/ only begins syllables; /ŋ/ never begins a word
short stressed vowels are followed by a consonant; open stressed syllables have long vowels or diphthongs
[ɡ] is marginal: it occurs between a sonorant and schwa (berge [ˈbærɡə]) and in loans

stress.type: lexical, mostly initial in native words
stress.rule: Native words stress the first syllable of the stem, the prefixes be-, ge-, ver-, ont-, er-, her- are unstressed, compounds stress their first member, and many loans keep final or penultimate stress (universiteit, banaan).
stress.cues: pitch movement, duration and vowel quality (unstressed syllables mostly have schwa); intensity is secondary

rhythm.vowel_reduction: strong: most unstressed syllables have schwa
rhythm.notes: I know of no published nPVI value for Afrikaans.

length.notes: Long /ɑː/ contrasts with short /a/; the other long monophthongs are marginal (before /r/, from contraction as in sê, môre, and in loans). The long mid vowels are diphthongs. There are no long consonants.

intonation.declarative: rises or peaks on accented syllables with a final fall to low on and after the last accent
intonation.wh_question: accent on the question word, final fall
intonation.continuation: rise or high level at the end of a non-final phrase
intonation.accent_shape: peak on the accented syllable followed by a fall
intonation.notes: Low confidence: the intonation of Afrikaans has been studied little, and these statements rest on the general descriptions and on the similarity to Dutch.

tone.notes: There is no lexical tone inventory. Coetzee et al. (2018) show that speakers differ in how often they prevoice /b d/, while all of them begin the following vowel on a clearly lower pitch after /b d/ than after /p t/, and that listeners use that pitch difference; the authors read this as tonogenesis under way. Reports of the same research give a difference of about 50 Hz at vowel onset and prevoicing in about 55 per cent of /b d/ for older and 15 per cent for younger speakers.

phonation: plosive voicing is being replaced by a pitch difference on the following vowel (lower after historically voiced /b d/)

problems: nasalised vowels keep the following [n] and are not lengthened: ons [õns], mens [mẽns], Afrikaans [ɐfrikˈɑ̃ns], where the language has [ɔ̃ːs], [mɛ̃ːs], [afriˈkɑ̃ːs]
/b d/ are always fully voiced and there is no pitch lowering after them, so the cue that carries the contrast for most present-day speakers is missing
ê outside the lowering contexts is close [eː] (sê, hê, gesê) where the language has open [ɛː]
/y/ is not lengthened before /r/ (vuur, muur, uur come out with the short vowel), although ie and oe are
dae and vrae lose their final schwa ([dɑː], [frɑː])
/l/ imports the English phoneme, clear before vowels, where Afrikaans has a velarised /l/ throughout
questions are given the same tune whether they are yes-no or wh-questions
good: the long mid vowels are centring diphthongs (been [biən], boom [bʊəm], seun [søən])
final devoicing is applied (hond [hɔnt], rib [rəp], brood [brʊət])
/ɛ/ is lowered to [æ] before k, g, l, r (ek, weg, vel, werk)
short i is schwa-like (kind [kənt]), short a is [ɐ] and long aa is [ɑː]
the diminutive has the palatal stop and the diphthongised vowel (katjie [kaɪci], hondjie [hɔɪŋci], the latter with a velar nasal where the language has a palatal one)
w is [w] after a consonant (twee, kwaad, swart) and [v] elsewhere; r is a trill
a large rule file with many stress exceptions; the voice is marked mature

notes: In the consonant list /ɡ dʒ z ʒ ʃ/ are marginal (loans and a few native contexts), [c] and [ɲ] arise from /k/, /t/ and /n/ before the diminutive ending, and [w] is the post-consonantal form of /v/. In the vowel list [æ æː] are lowered allophones of /ɛ ɛː/. The nasalised vowels [ɑ̃ː ɛ̃ː ɔ̃ː] are allophonic. No formant or voice onset time values are given because I cannot quote the published figures with confidence.
